definition: Blemish means a small imperfection on a surface — a mark that spoils the look while leaving the thing sound underneath.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word blemish. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know blemish should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The saddler works around every blemish in the hide rather than cutting through one.
A smudge is milder than a blemish — it wipes away and leaves the surface unharmed.
A gash goes further than a blemish: the surface itself is cut open, not merely marked.

A flaw is any defect at all, inside or out — a crack in a casting, a hole in an argument. A blemish stays on the surface: a small mark that spoils only the look of a thing while leaving it perfectly sound underneath.

Imperfection is the broadest, mildest word for falling short of perfect, and it needn't be visible at all — a wobbly chord, a rough draft. A blemish is specific: a small visible mark on an otherwise clean surface, skin, fruit, paint, or a reputation.

Old French ble(s)mir left exactly one descendant in modern English — blemish itself. Its root survives nowhere else, so there is no cousin word to build; the history lives in this single word for the mark an injury leaves.
Blemish means a small imperfection on a surface — a mark that spoils the look while leaving the thing sound underneath.
The used-car buyer circled the sedan twice and found a single blemish — a pea-sized dimple on the trunk lid — and talked four hundred dollars off the price for it.
Blemish is the precise word because the mark is small, superficial, and spoils only the look: the car runs perfectly.
A dent that changed how the trunk closed would be damage; a blemish just interrupts an otherwise clean surface.
Blemish is for small, surface-level faults — on skin, fruit, paint, or, figuratively, on a record or reputation.
If the defect runs deeper than the surface, flaw is the stronger, broader word; if it can simply be wiped away, it was only a smudge.

At the watch counter, Ruben's loupe went first to the dial, because a dial cannot be quietly fixed.
The 1962 chronograph in front of him ran perfectly — the movement serviced, the case square, every function crisp.
But at the edge of the dial, near the seven, sat a blemish the size of a pinhead: a pale spot where moisture had once kissed the lacquer.
It changed nothing about how the watch kept time.
It changed everything about the price.

'The inside is honest,' Ruben told the seller, 'but the eye lands there first.' He bought it anyway, at a third off, and sold it within a month to a collector who said he could live with one small mark on an otherwise clean face.
